> ˹commanding,˺ “Go to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺

**Idhhab: Two Letters That Found a Mission**

The call resolves into commission: *idhhab ilā firʿawn* — Go to Pharaoh. The imperative *idhhab* — Go — is the Book-historical ignition-verb of prophecy: the calls of the earlier messengers — Nouh, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ — organize themselves around this same mobilizing form, because prophetic careers in the Book begin as *movements*, not as opinions. The commission is short by design: no manual, no staff, no diplomatic cover; the man who came up the valley out of exile-shepherding is ordered: the target is the world's strongest throne — Go.

The fierceness of the send resides precisely in the simplicity: Go. Against the scale of Pharaoh's military-state, the command reads as implausible deportment — one exile versus an empire — but the commission has its own completed title: *your Lord* called him (79:16). Obedience to such a command depends only on the relationship named at the ledger preceding: where the caller is *your Lord*, the size of the commanded-target is already answered at the sentence's first syllable. God's messengers measure assignments by the Sender, not by the address.

**Ilā Firʿawn: The Target Named Without Cushions**

This naming-grammar is acted as therapy for the Messenger's own street: the Quraysh-leaders listening to this sūrah heard *Firʿawn* in their own flesh — the strong-man title of their own resistance — and the sūrah-story proceeds in fourteen verses to the end of Pharaoh inside the ocean and the afterlife. Prophetic stories in Meccan sūrahs perform their mapping first by *parallel noun*: each denier heard at once his name transcribed inside the ancient names — *I am your lord, the most high* entering Meccan ears from Egyptian mouths with Meccan inflections still on it (79:24).

**Innahu Ṭaghā: The Docket Against Him, One Verb**

One verb forms the whole charge: *innahu ṭaghā* — he has indeed transgressed, overflowed, exceeded. *Ṭaghā* is the flood-verb: a set out watercourse breaking banks, overflowing its proper route, expanding out beyond its channel into lands on which it has no claim. God's biography of the strongest ruler on earth condenses to this single water-verdict: overflow. All of Fire-risk analysis later in the Book, all of the Day-catastrophe the sūrah now opens at its end-verses, will classify its transgressors under this exact root — the ṭāghīn-file (78:22) is named from the same ṭ-gh-y stock as Pharaoh's docket.

**Why God Sends to the Vainest Man on Earth**

The speech-manner commanded is recorded in the parallel: *“Speak to him gently, so perhaps he may be mindful ˹of Me˺ or fearful”* (20:44) — *qawlān layyinan* — gentle speech, since even a man who drowned a generation of male children is given courtesy before the exit-genocide is wrought. The tradition since Moses has carried this commission as assignment-universal: call, gently, to the tyrants; invite with would-you's (79:18 uses one); then watch the record they make themselves. God's final difference with the tyrant always shows *first a calling*, and it is the calling that justifies the entire scaffolding of the seize that comes after.
verses.18:
> And say, ‘Would you ˹be willing to˺ purify yourself

**The Most Courteous Line Ever Spoken to Tyranny**

Here is the actual script of the Prophet's address to Pharaoh, and it begins with a question the Book has placed at the summit of courtesy: *fa-qūl hal laka ilā a tazakkā* — and say: Would you be inclined to purification? *Hal laka* — do you have — is Arabic's least coercive question-portal: the question asks the other if *he* has any share in the following purpose — if he *has it in him*, to partake of what is to be offered. At the court of the world's most violent monarch, God's messenger is told to open with: *would you have...?*

The phrasing is God's own pedagogy. The colossal distance between the two men — barefoot exile, throne-sovereign — is deliberately archived in the text with courtesy-of-manner inversely proportional to the power held, so that every follower of the calling reads the doctrine plainly: prophetic speech is not sized on threat-vector but on the addressee's would-be wellness. The crewed speech-order issued with it — *speak to him gently* (20:44) — completes the doctrine: gentle speech for the harsh-chinned, *would-you* for the insolence-crowned, from the mouths of people answered by no other shield than *their Lord* (79:16).

**Tazakkā: The Verb of Purification That Also Means Growth**

The tzadd's pragmatics, at the court of Pharaoh's achievement-show — his cities, his grain-silos, his temples — addressed his identity directly: you have spent so much on construction; would you wish to grow in purity? The offer does not seek mercy; it *flips the self-investment habit* of the builder-emperor onto the one field he had never sown; and his refusal-to-incline (79:21) will be narrated as the specific failure of this exact offer. The would-you form was chosen absolutely deliberately against the refusal it would meet: God instructs His envoy to ask — *would you have any inclination* — so that when Pharaoh does not, his *disinclination* is what the record seals.
verses.19:
> and let me guide you to your Lord so that you will be in awe ˹of Him˺?’”

**Ilā Rabbika: To YOUR Lord — The Pronoun of the Offended**

Three syllables install the redemption's axis: *ilā rabbika* — to your Lord. The possessive is deliberate and theologically loaded: even Pharaoh has a *rabb*. Even at the apex of self-overreach, the Pharaoh is *owned* by someone with the possessive right; and the prophet's diction confines the right to God: your Lord — not your despot, not you yourself: the addressee, to be guided-to, is already *his*. In the sūrah's own near-wording, the coming verse of the court-climax (79:24) will have Pharaoh cry, *I am your lord, the most high* — and the diction of verse 19 stands directly against it as the contended noun of the story: *rabb* — theirs in claim, His in fact.

**Fa-Takhshā: The Offer's Destination Is Awe**

And awe acts across all the Book as the parent of all tags-closing virtues: at the sūrah's own closing explicitly, the file-division marks the two kinds of men by the presence or absence of this awe: *those who were in awe of standing before their Lord* (79:40) gets the garden-estate; the *ṭāghūn* and *world-preferrers* get the fire-estate (79:37-39). The offer to Pharaoh was so literally an offer at the exact station of the final fork: *learn awe now* — and the next verses map his disinclination to it into his permanent placement at the other estate.

It should be limpid from the whole record what God's pre-knowledge of Pharaoh's response was; the gentle-offer was issued *knowing* the answer. That is one of the Book's most chilling pedagogy-points: calls given-knowing-their-answers are not gambles; they are *establishments*. To hold out the purification-offer to the destined rejecter is God's declared way of full-establishing the argument against him (hujja) so that the tyrant's seize-verse (79:25) and its closing moral at 79:26 will be complete: the lesson against the awe-worthy needs the offer to have come first.

The Book keeps this pattern throughout: offers reach the greats refused-takers with full divine knowledge of their response. Prophets are ordered the *perhaps* — speak gently so perhaps he may be mindful (20:44) — a perhaps from the All-Knowing's own prescription, issued to us as instruction in hope: divine speech operates in *perhaps* not because God is uncertain but because the office of the warners must be run on the probabilities as experienced — and the warner must call without ever being taught beforehand which addressee will decline. Pharaoh answered in the negative; another, somewhere along the call's recitation down the ages, might answer in the affirmative: *perhaps* — God's mercy of the *perhaps* keeps every would-you open.

**And to Complete the Offer, the Sign Will Be Shown**

The call's accompaniment arrives next with its visible flank: the great sign (79:20). Gentle-speech + offered guidance + awe-destination is God's court-protocol as far as its speech-side goes; then the evidence-side of the same protocol: the staff, the hand — the sign that turns dependent-men away from its full interior need, as every audience returns after that either with awe or with self-summitry's claim.
verses.20:
> Then Moses showed him the great sign

**Fa-Arāhu: The Evidence Is Staged**

The call completed its speech-side; now its evidence-side proceeds: *fa-arāhu l-āyata l-kubrā* — and he showed him the great sign. The showing-verb is deliberate: *arā* is display, presentation, the making-visible: the sign is not told about or argued; it is *held up*, in the court, in full view of the throne and its jurists. Prophecy's method is established in the one verb: invitation first (vv17-19), display next — the warner's gentleness is then backed by the Sender's demonstration.

**Deny First, Then Disobey — The Response Verse Arrives**

The bridge into verse 21 is the turn of the episode into its moral second act: from here forward the sūrah narrates only what Pharaoh's own machinery added to himself after the sign: turning, striving, summoning, crying *I am your lord most high*. The display-verse so stands at the hinge of the whole episode: before it, God's participatory movement toward mercy (call, invitation, guide, sign); after it, Pharaoh's machine, unchecked, by its own filename (79:22's striving). The briefest sign-verse leads so into the wildest passage of self-monarchy in sacred history — the summit-claim — and the most documented seizure, both of which belong to the sūrah's closing anatomy of transgression's biographies.
verses.21:
> but he denied and disobeyed ˹Allah˺

**He Rejected and Disobeyed**

The verse says that Pharaoh denied the truth and disobeyed. The two words are paired on purpose, and between them they cover what a person can do with a message: he can say it is not true, and he can refuse to act on it.

**What Denial Means Here**

The man described in the verse had the sign in front of him. Moses had come with the staff and the hand, and he had spoken plainly; the verse does not say Pharaoh lacked information, and the next verse says he turned away and set about opposing Moses (79:22 gives the two acts). The Book uses the same description elsewhere for people who reject what they can see, and the tradition gave that kind of denial a name of its own: the refusal of something the man knows in his heart is true. He was not working out whether the message was right; he had decided what he wanted the answer to be.

**Why He Wanted That Answer**

The sūrah has already described Pharaoh's position. Moses had offered him a way out and invited him to purify himself and to fear God (79:19 records the invitation), and the cost of accepting was everything the man had built: the throne, the court, the temples and the worship of the river. When he asked whether he was the lord most high, he was not asking a question (79:24 records his claim). The Book shows the same kind of trade in other stories, where men calculate what faith would cost them and then call the message false.

**The Other Side of the Account**

The sūrah puts the two reactions beside each other so that the reader can see what is at stake. The sūrah of the News says the same about the two roads: it describes the men who did not expect an account and denied the signs (78:27 and 78:28 name the two things), and then says that the man who rebelled and preferred this life will have his home in the fire, while the man who feared standing before his Lord and held himself back from his desires will have the garden (79:40 and 79:41 state the two ends). The two words in front of the reader, denial and disobedience, are the exact pair that the sūrah answers at its close.

**What the Verse Teaches the Reader**

The verse teaches the reader what unbelief looks like when it is stripped of excuses. It is not usually a person who has weighed the evidence and found it lacking; it is a person who has decided what he wants to be true and then argues backwards. The sūrah ends with the same test in a different form, and it tells the reader that the two things which save a person are the fear of standing before God and the refusal to follow his own appetite. The verse in front of the reader is the negative picture of both. The sūrah's own account of the men who did not expect an account and denied the signs stands just before this passage (78:27) and (78:28) state the two things, and the verse before the reader is the same pair of acts in one man's life.
verses.22:
> then turned his back, striving ˹against the truth˺

**The Parallel of the Efforting-Against-Truth Class**

The striving-lone word deserves its own systemic note in the Book's anthropology: elsewhere when mankind *strives*, the saʿy-word carries positive names (the labour toward God, pilgrimage-ḥajj-saʿy). The same verb on Ṭā for its target is the tragedy: *effort exists* — human possibility is not the issue — effort permanently solvable; sin's matter is never capacity but *aim*: all capacity found expedited down the wrong channel: saʿy against the truth. The Book elsewhere memorializes such striving against the signs of the Messenger with the same register: those who strive against our signs, racing ahead (34:38's expression), is a fixed head-count of the Book's outlaw-file.

**Yasʿā: It Was Labour, Not Leisure**

And what comes next is more terrible than denial itself: he *strove* — yasʿā from *saʿy*: purposeful running, striving-forward. Not passive withdrawal of credence; busy, organized, labour-grade assault on the consequences of the sight. The tradition reads the verb as the mad-dream of the court: the consultation-with-chiefs, the accusation-engine (he is a sorcerer), the summons of every proficient magician in the Nile-valley, the contest-appointments, the arrangements — a full departmental effort to falsify the Sign by outproducing it.

The striving-verb specifies for us the *industry of rejection*: ṭughyān responds to evidence not with greater ease but with *effort*: a new mythology is produced. The media-division is mobilized; every resource of the regime's court is justly named saʿy — running-effort, labor — the tyrant sprints harder at disproving God's light than he ever hearkened to incline toward purity. The paradox of sin at scale: the man who would not turn one inch to purification (79:18) runs miles to destroy the evidence offered *to* him.

**Why Turned Away Instead of Attacked Directly**

And the Book's own physiology of such scenes is consistent elsewhere: the deniers in the same act-of-turning the back at signs dispatched to them — hearing inattention (18:57 reports heedlessness-turned-away; 46:3's turning away); reaching the same structure: the crowd that cannot look long at what condemns them averts itself, turns the physical back as the last defensive wall against vision that is still operative. The back-turned silhouette of a throne was measured once by the drops of the Nile-vision: the king has already left the verdict to the paying-tellers under the tent of the magicians' arrival (79:23 next).
verses.23:
> Then he summoned ˹his people˺ and called out

**Fa-Nādā: The Loud Proclamation as State Signal**

Then *fa-nādā* — he cried out, proclaimed loudly. The cry-verb is exactly the same verb-family that governs God's own call: He *called* Moses in the valley; the sūrah-system of nādā ends both voices' contrast: *this* calling is at stadium-volume for a false declaration, the valley's calling was intimate for a true one (79:16). Loudness of proclamation does not trade for truth; rather — and this is a permanent Qur'anic lesson about propaganda — crowds and loud cries are the native costume of self-authored claims. The word is call; and *Ḥashr plus nādā* is the formula for the fabricated messiah-event: an audience assembled not by truth but by herald-power.

**Rivalry Mocked by the Very Vocabulary**

The irony ripens in the last comparison the sūrah will allow: the Day of decisive assembly (79:6-14, 34-36) is headed by *The* King with the valid Muster and the valid Caller. Afterward, no bragging assembly of any transgressor is available for leverage. And the chiefs and subject-crowds stand at the plain with no heralds between — where Pharaoh's drama shall content itself with a footnote in the annals read by judges who outrank him (78:38 operational in the family too: ranks and licensed speech).

**The Crowd-Conditioned Audience as Witness Against Itself**

The ḥashr-material also equips the account with witnesses: assemblies gather proof. Had Pharaoh's no stayed a private-vice, few in Egypt would have known how the sign was answered. The Leader open-mic cry delivered in a packed assembly filled contemporaneous Egypt with the evidence of its claim — so that when the takedown came (vv25-26), there was no village later to plead insufficient advance knowledge of what had been claimed. The summoned crowd — will or nil — was made co-attending at the unTruth of its King.
verses.24:
> saying, “I am your lord, the most high!”

**The word al-Aʿlā and the Sūrah's Own Argument**

The superlative-adjective is precisely theologically placed in the sūrah's own vocabulary of God: *He built the sky, raising it high* (79:27-28), *He is most high* in the Book's attributes; the Book's custody of *al-aʿlā* belongs to the Throned one, upraised, He alone (cf. The neighbouring sūrah of al-Aʿlā itself, the 87th, sealed by the direct cognate pair at v16-17 about preferring the world). The claim by the Nile-king to be *al-aʿlā* is so an usurpation not just of obedience-territory but of *attribute-territory*: he is borrowing throne-adjectives of heaven's king for fast-food crowns.

**The Pathology as Worked Anatomy**

Held up as a case-study, the proclamation is the final shape of the overflow-lineage: desire for standing (79:22's striving) becomes *claim* for godship: what the human begins as self-concern ends as self-theology. There may not be one reader earned without noticing how every stage of his story was one metre to this: every rise of class, wealth, or applause a further production-index for the same sound-byte. The adornment of lifestyles and titles in every age is the carbon monologue of the same pathology — to upgrade rank-credit until one day the man speaks *I* where *He* should hold the sentence.

Al-Rāzī's era-time readers wrote the humanistic moral: Egypt did not produce this madness as single-cause; ḥashr and nādā and rank and years of un-restrained applause built the tunnel by which an ordinary man came to say *I am your lord, the most high* without flinching. The sūrah pre-also-recites the same lesson in pronoun-psychology: *you* (vv 10-11) is a pronoun unkempt by any *rabb*, and before long ego builds to a self-crowned form; or it can be held by awe — and self stays in its creature-size, the mould of peace (79:40).

**Every Pharaonic Forum Rehearsed Against Every Recitation**

For the Meccan street, this claim arrives embedded in its own present-tense: senior chiefs had been giving their speeches too, named-standing heights, sworn-in words; God-claims mitigated with easy polytheist conference-speak. Quraysh heard in *ana rabbukumu l-aʿlā* the formal maximal of every supremacy act on their own network: the argumentative function of the archive goes right past its story-context, since the sūrah's closing preserves *his name, not their names*. *classifies* them with ṭaghā (79:37: *who transgressed* — using the same ṭughyān as the charge against him at 79:17).

The argument also stands, inexorably, for all future audiences: rulers, media-tsars, celebrity-self gods, idea-Nile apologists — *ana rabbukum* re-appears in every epochal form — and the sūrah answers them all with the same seizure-verse (79:25) that is coming now: God's docketing of the claimants by the two-world counter. Still: benchmark of the Book's law: any claim that takes for man what belongs to God inherits the judgment against the author of the claim in the primary record; and the file-end of that pathology is written within the next breath (v25).
verses.25:
> So Allah overtook him, making him an example in this life and the next

**Fa-Akhadhahu Llāh: The Answer Arrives**

One verb performs the whole flood: *fa-akhadhahu llāhu nakāla l-ākhirati wal-ūlā* — so Allah seized him — the seizing of the next life and the first. *Akhadh* is grasp/capture: the vocabulary of laying hold, sudden and inescapable; the *fa-* connector closes the causality: after the most-high proclamation, *so* Allah seized him. The seizure carries no naming of logistics here; the Book's seizing-files keep that register — the grip is named; the events follow in other passages; here it is stated, not narrated, because the audience knows the story: at the water's edge, the crown went under, confessing too late.

**Matching the Claim: Aʿlā Against Akhira and Ūlā**

Finally the verse's *nakāl* construction bears a lexical counter-fitting of exactness that no alert reader misses: the claimed superlative *al-aʿlā* — Most High — is faced by the double *al-ākhirati wal-ūlā* — the Next and the First — the two titles that God appropriates for Himself among His revealed names: *He is the First and the Last*. Equivalence-flavored revenge is God's documentary habit (the fitting-wage of ch78); here the claim most-HIGH is toppled by a seizure signed by the One who signs His own bio as first-last — the heights of Pharaoh's self-projections towered and were flattened inside the two frames that summarize real highness.
verses.26:
> Surely in this is a lesson for whoever stands in awe of ˹Allah˺

**Dhālika: The Demonstrative That Carries an Archive**

Notice what the pointer-word *dhālika* (in that) is made to hold. A demonstrative pronoun, one of the lightest particles in the language's toolkit, is here loaded with the entire four-act drama: the gentle call at the sacred valley, the offer of purification and guidance, the great sign displayed, the sneer of supremacy, the gathering, the claim, the seizure. An entire archive compressed into a pointing finger. This loading of the small with the immense is characteristic of the sūrah's economy: five-word verses that carry the resurrection ("a single Shout" in v13), a three-word answer that carries creation's whole workshop ("He built it," in v27). The concentration is itself instructive. Revelation does not need bulk to carry weight; it needs exact placement. When the pointer lands — *in that* — everything narrated since v15 stands behind it in a single rank, marshalled into one exhibit. The listener who has been following the drama at walking pace suddenly finds the whole march reviewed in one glance, and the glance is the point: the story seen whole, as a shape, is the lesson the story in pieces could not quite deliver.

**The Seal Placed on Stories Throughout the Book**

This closing technique — narrate, then declare the narrative's function aloud — runs through the revelation like a manufacturer's stamp. In one sweeping statement: "And We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the stories of the messengers to reassure your heart. And there has come to you in this ˹sûrah˺ the truth, a warning ˹to the disbelievers˺, and a reminder to the believers." (11:120) Steadying, warning, reminding — the three offices of narrated precedent — are all discharged by these eleven verses of the sūrah. The Prophet's heart is steadied: the enemy he faces belongs to a species whose most powerful specimen is already waterlogged. The deniers are warned: the machinery of seizure is older and stronger than their confederacy. The believers are reminded: endurance has precedent, and precedent has a drowning-pool.

Having grounded its argument in the soils of Egyptian precedent, the sūrah lifts its audience's chin: "Which is harder to create: you or the sky?" (79:27). The pivot is tactical.
verses.27:
> Which is harder to create: you or the sky? He built it

**Which Is Harder to Create: The Interrogation of Scale**

The opening construction — *are you more formidable as a creation, or the sky?* — is a forced comparison elegantly rigged. The adjective *ashaddu* (harder, more vehement, more intensely wrought) is a human-feeling word, borrowed from the audience's own instinct about what counts as a difficult object; the question enlists their native judgment as the measuring instrument. No abstract theology is requested yet — only a comparison of workmanship, the kind of judgment a craftsman delivers about two artefacts. Yet the comparison is loaded the moment it is asked. On one side stands the listener: a body, a span of years, a grave's worth of matter.

**Banāhā: Three Letters That Finish the Debate**

Then the answer drops, and its brevity is the punch: "He built it." Whatever verdict the audience reached about the sky's difficulty, the building-permit for the sky already carries His name. The sūrah's sister-passage makes the same attribution with architectural specificity about layered firmament, "and built above you seven mighty ˹heavens˺," (78:12), giving the construction its storeys.

**Arguing From the Greater Down to the Lesser**

This is the classic logic of the greater implying the lesser, turned on the resurrection-doubter with unusual bluntness. The sneer recorded earlier — "Will we really be restored to our former state" (79:10) — rested on an intuition about impossibility: decay looks like an one-way process, and restoration looks like a demand exceeding any plausible budget of power. The verse confiscates that intuition by re-pricing the budget. The relevant comparison is not between a living body and a rotten one; it is between a body and the sky. Whoever concedes that the vault overhead is fabricated — and the verse permits no third option, asking *which* of the two is harder, not *whether* either is fabricated — has already conceded a workshop whose capacity dwarfs the complaint. Restoration shrinks, on this scale, from miraculous exception to routine maintenance.

**Raised, and Finished Well**

The line's own continuation begins the specification: "raising it high and forming it flawlessly." (79:28). Two workmanship-verbs will now carry the detail — elevation as deliberate act, completion without warp — and behind them the challenge the Book issues elsewhere, inviting every generation to audit the dome for defects and report back. The sky, in other words, is about to be walked through as a building inspection. The builder of a body hidden in a mother's dark is also the roofer of the visible world; the sneerer's doubt about the dark-work falls, plank by plank, as the roof-work is described above his head.
verses.28:
> raising it high and forming it flawlessly

**Rafaʿa Samkahā: The Vault Lifted by Decision**

The noun *samk* names the upper reach of a thing — its roof, its height-curve — and the verb *rafaʿa* declares that this reach was hoisted, not drifted into. The language insists on deliberateness: a lifter raised it, the way a builder raises a ridge-beam, the way a tent-master hauls a canopy onto its poles, though with no poles at all — a suspension none of the audience's builders could imitate on any budget. Height here is not descriptive background but product: distance between floor and ceiling was itself manufactured. This matters for the argument underway. A sky that simply happened to be far could be dismissed as luck of arrangement; a sky *raised* belongs to a campaign of construction, with intent readable in the gap between earth and vault.

**Flawlessness Under Cross-Examination**

The Book does not leave the claim of perfection as decorative praise; it converts it into an auditable challenge. Then look again and again— your sight will return frustrated and weary." (67:3-4) There is the test protocol in full: look, look again, look until the eyes tire, and record what the inspection finds.

**And the Light Is Managed Next**

The construction report continues into the management of what plays beneath the vault: "He dimmed its night, and brought forth its daylight." (79:29). The same hand that raised the canopy also runs the lighting beneath it — dimming and summoning, scheduling the darkness and the blaze.
verses.29:
> He dimmed its night, and brought forth its daylight

**Aghṭasha Laylahā: Darkness as Something Administered**

The verb *aghṭasha* means to darken, to dim, to draw the deep shade over; its startling implication is that night is a product, not a residue. The common instinct treats darkness as light's mere absence — what remains when the lamp fails, owing nothing to anyone. The verse reassigns ownership: the dark is *dimmed in*, administered, drawn like a curtain by hand at the proper hour. And the Book elsewhere certifies the motive of the administration as mercy: "It is out of His mercy that He has made for you the day and night so that you may rest ˹in the latter˺ and seek His bounty ˹in the former˺, and perhaps you will be grateful." (28:73). Rest engineered into the schedule; recovery built into the planet's rotation; the body's nightly repair-shifts staffed by the dimming itself. A world of unbroken glare would exhaust its creatures within days — poets in every latitude have intuited the gift of the dark without knowing its invoice. This verse delivers the invoice: the mercy that dims the lamps each night, on time, for uncounted sleepers, is the same mercy whose household the sneerers deny exists.

**The Alternation as a Twice-Daily Rehearsal**

What makes the cycle evidentiary is precisely its repeatability. Elsewhere the Book stamps the same daily swap with its standard verdict: "He covers the day with night. Surely in this are signs for those who reflect." (13:3). Signs — plural, recurring, located in the regularity itself. A one-time marvel could be archived as anomaly; a marvel on a twenty-four-hour loop becomes curriculum. The alternation is the classroom where reflection keeps being re-enrolled: each dusk re-poses the question of who dims, each dawn re-poses the question of who draws forth, and the accumulated repetitions build the case with the slow force of a sediment. Notably, the verse assigns no mechanism-language, no physics; it assigns agents and verbs.

**Night and Day in This Sūrah's Sister-Inventory**

The alternation appears again within the parallel chapter the audience has just been reciting, priced in the currency of use: the dark drawn down "and made the night as a cover," (78:10) — the cover-metaphor matching this verse's curtain-drawing — and the bright half set to work "and made the day for livelihood," (78:11). The two passages cross-reference each other like twin ledgers kept in one hand: the same Auditor listing the same fixtures, from slightly different angles, a chapter apart. Such internal rhyme is not redundancy; it is the Book's signature method of rendering its claims checkable. A reader who heard the earlier chapter finds its fixtures re-certified here under construction-vocabulary; a reader who starts here meets mercy-economics in the other. The alternation also quietly indicts: the sneerers schedule their plowing, their caravans, their evening councils by this exact dimming and out-bringing — their entire calendar is subcontracted from the schedule they mock. Tenants run their livelihoods on the landlord's lighting rota while disputing the landlord's existence.

**After the Roof, the Deck**

The tour of construction descends a floor: "As for the earth, He spread it out as well," (79:30). The same passage that lifted the vault now unrolls the ground beneath it — the deck spread for occupancy after the roof was raised.
verses.30:
> As for the earth, He spread it out as well

**Baʿda Dhālika: A Delicate Question of Sequence**

The words *after that* prompted the commentators to careful work, since the Book elsewhere narrates the earth's making before the heavens' forming in seven stages — "So He formed the heaven into seven heavens in two Days, assigning to each its mandate." (41:12) — following there upon the earth's own accounting. The reconciling instinct of the tradition took *after* here as an order of display and rank rather than a strict clock: the earth, existing from the first campaign, receives its final spreading-out and furnishing after the heaven's erection — the deck completed, once the roof stood over it. Whatever the harmonization adopted, the verse's own emphasis is unmistakable: the spreading is a later *finish*, a commissioning, distinct from raw existence. The ground was there; then it was *made ready* — rolled flat for feet, opened for springs, prepared for seed. Read this way, the small phrase deserts chronology-quarrels and joins the verse's real theme: the earth is not only present; it is *prepared* — and preparation is the signature of intention. A campsite found is luck; a campsite laid is hospitality. The verb *daḥā* belongs to the vocabulary of spreading wide, flattening out, extending level — and the Arabs heard in it images from their own landscape, among them the ostrich smoothing and widening its nest-bed in the sand: a broad, worked patch of ground, deliberately prepared for what will be laid and hatched upon it. A bird's nest-bed is not spectacular; it is *serviceable* — and that is exactly the register in which the verse wants the earth's expanses heard.

**The Look-At-It Imperative of the Parallel Chapter**

The Book elsewhere turns this same fact into a direct command to stare: "and the earth—how it was levelled out?" (88:20). The interrogative *how* is doing the work of a whole treatise — by what flattening, what rolling, what grading was the crust of a fire-balled planet rendered meadowable and roadable? The twin passages share the Book's characteristic move: take the most over-familiar datum in experience and prosecute it with a question mark until it confesses. Levelled out *how* — and for whom?

**Then the Utilities: Water and Grass**

A spread deck is still only potential until its services run, and the next line switches them on: "bringing forth its water and pastures" (79:31). The out-bringing verb returns — the same extraction-verb that drew forth the morning blaze now draws the earth's hidden stores: water summoned to the surface, grazing summoned out of dust.
verses.31:
> bringing forth its water and pastures

**Akhraja Minhā Māʾahā: Water Summoned From the Ground**

The phrase's architecture rewards attention: He brought forth *from it* — from the just-spread earth — its water. The vital fluid's location is the marvel: stored *in* the ground, in darkness, beyond the reach of any bucket technology until released — and then released *from it*, as if the deck were a cistern with a Keeper's tap. The Book's parallel inventories return to this extraction repeatedly: gardens and "caused springs to gush forth in it," (36:34) — springs, the very image of water *brought out*, pressurized up from concealment into daylight. The audience knew wells: pits sunk on hope, brackish yields, the water-table as rumor. Against that anxious economics of access, the verse declares the whole planetary waterworks an administered dispensing — rain received, stored, filtered through rock, and re-issued at spring-mouths and river-heads on a schedule no tribe manages. The extraction-verb is exact: not created-on-the-spot each time, but *brought forth*, released from appointed holding. Hydrology here is payroll: reserves under management, issuance on time, for populations that never see the accounts office.

**The Book's Command to Examine One's Own Mouthful**

The parallel chapter that opens with the human food-supply issues a blunt imperative: "Let people then consider their food:" (80:24) — and then tracks the sequence: rain split open, earth furrowed, grain and grape, fodder and fruit, descending the chain item by item to the mouth. This verse is the compressed form of that entire audit: water and pasture, the chain's two foundational links, named in five words as extractions to be examined. The imperative's significance deserves emphasis: the Book does not merely *state* providence; it instructs its hearers to perform the audit themselves, to conduct the inspection at their own tables and trace the mouthful backward through pasture and water to the extraction-verb. Such an audit is falsifiable-in-principle, inspectable, walkable: the wells are there, the grazing arrives, the chains run.

**A Cycle That Preaches Return From Death**

The pasture has one more office in the Book's curriculum: it dies and returns. The golden, then the dust-dry, then — after rain — the green again: the dead-earth revival is the standing visual aid for the sūrah's disputed claim. The Book says so outright: "There is a sign for them in the dead earth: We give it life, producing grain from it for them to eat." (36:33).

**Then the Anchors of the Deck**

One utility remains before the purpose-clause lands: "and setting the mountains firmly ˹upon it˺—" (79:32). The spread deck, like any broad fabric, must be held down against its own restlessness, and the fastening-instruments are the most violent-looking objects on the landscape — the mountains, here named as the settled anchors of the rolling earth. The construction tour moves from utilities to fasteners, and then, with the whole edifice standing, the verse after will name what all of it was *for*.
verses.32:
> and setting the mountains firmly ˹upon it˺—

**Wal-Jibāla Arsāhā: The Anchoring Verb**

The verb *arsā* carries the sense of setting firm, of anchoring into stability — its root (r-s-y) runs through the language wherever restlessness is brought to rest, where a vessel at anchor stops dragging, where a structure's sway is killed by its seating. Applying such a verb to mountains performs a deliberate shock of reclassification: the objects an audience experiences as the ultimate un-moved movers of the landscape are described as *themselves moved into place* — seated, settled, installed. Once that reclassification lands, the mountains' look changes: their massiveness stops reading as the earth's own brute necessity and starts reading as *work*, the deliberate emplacement of exactly the right counterweights for exactly this deck. The image underneath is of a spread expanse that must be held: fabric pinned at intervals so wind and ripple cannot take it. The most violent-looking formation in nature, on this telling, is the landscape's mooring system. Nothing in observation contradicts the description; every later science that has mapped the crust's restlessness has only deepened what the verb already said.

**Firmness Against the Trembling of the Floor**

The Book states the mountains' stabilizing office in so many words, more than once. "He has placed into the earth firm mountains, so it does not shake with you, as well as rivers, and pathways so you may find your way." (16:15).

**The Pegs of the Sister-Chapter Reappear**

This sūrah's immediate predecessor had already filed the mountains under their homeliest metaphor: "and ˹made˺ the mountains as ˹its˺ pegs," (78:7) — tent-pegs, the Bedouin's fastening of choice, the driven hold-fast on which a camp's whole shelter depends. Peg in one chapter, anchored-seating in the next: the imagery varies, the attribution and function stay identical, and the identity is itself an argument. Two audiences, two passage-architectures, one Inventory — the fixtures match across the chapters the way twin manifest-copies match in one clerk's hand. For the listening Meccans, the peg-image would have landed first: every one of them had struck a tent-peg and trusted a shelter to it. Now the recitation offers the engineering register above the domestic one: not just pegs, but *settled anchors*, seated with finality. The mountain you watch on the horizon is a fastening the Builder drove, and — the metaphor's quiet extension — if the world's very deck is pegged down by His hand, the notion of slipping His grasp on any Day is carpentry-naïve. What He stakes, stays.

**Now the Purpose of the Whole Edifice**

Vault, alternation, deck, water, pasture, anchors — the assemblage stands complete, and the next line names its destination: "all as ˹a means of˺ sustenance for you and your animals." (79:33). The entire majestic inventory folds into one word of provision and one pair of beneficiaries.

And again, in the prophets' chapter: "And We have placed firm mountains upon the earth so it does not shake with them, and made in it broad pathways so they may find your way." (21:31).
verses.33:
> all as ˹a means of˺ sustenance for you and your animals

**Matāʿan: A Word of Provision With an Expiry Inside It**

The word *matāʿ* names goods-for-use: provision, convenience, the serviceable stuff of life — yet the Book's wider usage has dyed the term with temporariness: matāʿ is what you hold for a term, enjoyment-ware with its limit built in. Both tones sound here. As provision, the word dignifies the whole inventory: sky and earth and their works exist *as* service, delivered; the cosmos is not indifferent scenery but stocked equipment. As temporary-use, it quietly posts the expiry: this splendid assemblage is *interim*, a running facility, and facilities close. The Book elsewhere uses exactly this vocabulary to draw exactly this conclusion: "These are the pleasures of this worldly life, but with Allah is the finest destination." (3:14). The pleasures are real — matāʿ is not illusion — and precisely because real, their service-status matters: sustenance is a means, and means exist toward ends beyond themselves. To confuse the facility with the destination is the exact error the sūrah will shortly attach to its doomed class. The stock is lavish; the stock is interim; both halves of the definition must be carried together.

**The Identical Line, Twice-Certified in the Book**

Here is a fact of the text too striking to pass over: this closing line appears again, word for word, elsewhere — "all as ˹a means of˺ sustenance for you and your animals." (80:32) — sealing the parallel chapter's own cosmic-food audit. Identical purpose-clauses cap two separate provisioning inventories, like a clerk's standard endorsement stamped on two files in succession. The repetition is a pedagogy of emphasis: the Book's refrain-engineering ensures that no attentive reciter can march through either passage without arriving at, and retaining, the identical destination. There is also an interlock-argument available to any reader who reflects: two chapter-contexts, differently built, converging on the same sentence — testimony to the single authorship supervising both files, drawing both inventories into one doctrine of provision.

**Provision-Irony: The sūrah's Standing Theme Restated**

This tilts the verse toward irony, and the sūrah has been cultivating the irony from its opening. The sister-chapter's version of the same audit was even more explicit about the supply-lines of the denial: rain sent down, grain and gardens issued — "and sent down from rainclouds pouring water," (78:14) — while the Day that will audit the ledgers is dismissed as fantasy.

**Then the Cover-All Arrives**

The provision-contract has an audit-date, and the recitation turns to it without transition-mercy: "But, when the Supreme Disaster comes to pass—" (79:34). The same creation that stands stacked here as service will stand re-categorized at that arrival; the matāʿ-hour expires; the ledger of provision becomes available as the ledger of evidence. The tenants who filled the purpose-clause will meet the Purpose-Giver's settlement-day, prepared or unprepared, stocked only with what they sent ahead. The sūrah has brought its audience from oath to the order of the universe to lunch-table; it will now bring them, in three strikes, to the bifurcation of every striving underneath that roof.
verses.34:
> But, when the Supreme Disaster comes to pass—

**Another Name for the Day**

By this point the sūrah has collected several names for the Day, each pointing at a different part of its terror. It opened with the quaking, named by the shaking of the ground (79:6 names it). It waited inside a single Shout, named by the call that raises (79:13 names it). Here it arrives as the Cover-All, named by the overwhelming spread of what covers. Quaking below, a shout above, water rising over everything. The multiplication of names is deliberate teaching about the Last Day. A reality too large for one name is described through many, and each name renews the warning against a different kind of deafness. A heart unmoved by the quaking may still hear the summons.

**What Happens When It Comes**

The sūrah records what a human being does at that moment. He remembers what he worked for (79:35 states it), and the blazing fire is brought out for anyone who can see (79:36 describes it). So the name given in this verse is not decoration. It is the last warning before the account is opened, and it comes with the memory of a lifetime's work arriving all at once.

**How the Book Names This Day Elsewhere**

In the verses around this one, the Day is described by its effect on people as much as by its own appearance. Elsewhere the Book says that every person will come on that Day with a driver and a witness (50:21 describes it), and that death will find a person wherever he is, even in towers built to keep it out (4:78 states it). The sūrah uses that same method: name the event, then show what it does to the people standing under it, so that the name and the memory and the fire all arrive together as one warning.
verses.35:
> the Day every person will remember all ˹their˺ striving

**Yawma Yatadhakkaru: The Grammar of Compelled Recall**

The verb *yatadhakkaru* — he will remember, he will recollect — carries in its form the sense of strenuous, reflective re-collection: not a passing thought but the mind *assembling* what was filed, re-collecting the scattered into one view. In this world, memory is the mercy of drift: deeds fade, embarrassments blur, the long-ago becomes anecdote. The Day verb announces the end of drift. Recall becomes *compelled* — total, orderly, and involuntary, like an archive whose locks all release at once under the Keeper's order. The significance for the proceedings is deep: the judgment requires no external projector to establish the facts. Each witness carries the footage, and the Day's first ruling is that the footage plays. This also reframes earthly forgetfulness: what the sneerers comfort themselves by forgetting is not erased, only *deferred*, filed in the very vault of the self that will, on command, open.

What gets remembered is specified by the same verb the sūrah used for the tyrant's record: *saʿā* — "then turned his back, striving ˹against the truth˺." (79:22). The striving-word is deliberate universalization.

**The Twin Verse Where Remembering Breaks Into Regret**

The Book owns an exact twin for this verse, in which the recall and its consequence unfold in one breath: "and Hell is brought forth on that Day—this is when every ˹disbelieving˺ person will remember ˹their own sins˺. But what is the use of remembering then? They will cry, 'I wish I had sent forth ˹something good˺ for my ˹true˺ life.'" (89:23-24). The twin adds the two beats this verse leaves implicit: the uselessness of recall that arrives after the lock-out. The cry it rips out — *what is the use of remembering then?* Remembering is salvation's organ while it can still edit behavior; post-lockout, the same organ is punishment's whip, because it only replays. Note the wish's precise grammar: *sent forth* — the regretter does not wish he had *been* different in some vaporous sense but that he had *capital forwarded*, good dispatched ahead of him like provision posted to the future address he now occupies.

**Then the Exhibit Is Unscreened Before Every Eye**

Recall is private; what follows is public: "and the Hellfire will be displayed for all to see—" (79:36). The interior archive having been read, the exterior destination is unveiled — exposed in open view, for every eye in the muster.
verses.36:
> and the Hellfire will be displayed for all to see—

The verb *burrizat* — from a root meaning to come out into the open ground, to be fully disclosed in the clear space — carries a theatrical exactness: something long kept behind partitions is now staged with none. The Fire had been the most scoffed-at item in the preaching precisely because it was unseeable; deniers trade on the invisibility of the warned-of, and every sneer in the sūrah's earlier movement drew credit from the fact that no blaze could be subpoenaed into a Meccan assembly. Note the divine passive: no agent need be pictured hauling it forth — the grammatical form is the pure event, the exposure *happening*, as if curtains simply cease to exist.

**The Twin Verse: Brought Forth on That Day**

The Book's parallel scene uses a companion verb from the same family of forced emergence — "and Hell is brought forth on that Day" (89:23) — and there the emergence is explicitly sequential: first the Lord comes for judgment, then the ranks are formed, then the Fire is hauled into view, then the remembering and the regret-break. Such twin attestations do the Book's usual double duty.

**The Pass-Over Decree That Includes Everyone**

How total is this exposure? The Book's most sweeping statement makes the sighting — even the crossing — an universal decree: "There is none of you who will not pass over it. ˹This is˺ a decree your Lord must fulfil. Then We will deliver those who were devout, leaving the wrongdoers there on their knees." (19:71-72). None exempt; decree framed as *must-fulfil*; and the differentiation reserved for the passage's second half: deliverance for the devout, kneeling for the wrongdoers. The display of this verse is therefore not a spectacle merely for the damned — it functions differently for the two great classes who witness it.

**Then the Two Files Are Called by Name**

With the exhibit standing in open view, the sorting proceeds by the grammar of *as-for*: "then as for those who transgressed" (79:37). The crowd of the muster — every soul now seer of the Fire — is re-filed by two markers only: transgression joined to world-preference on one side, majesty-awe joined to desire-restraint on the other. The next five verses perform the entire bifurcation of the species in two mirrored sentences, each ending with its own *certainly* and its own *home*. The display was the common evidence before both benches; what differs is what each file did with its striving — and the verse-by-verse exercise that follows shows how little, in the end, separates the two records: one preference, one restraint, and the distance between two homes.
verses.37:
> then as for those who transgressed

**Fa-Ammā: The Sorter's Particle**

The construction *fa-ammā...* — *then as for...* — is the language's machinery for partitioning a whole into addressed cases: a holder of many files opens one and says, *now, this one*. Paired shortly with its sibling (*and as for...*), it will exhaust the assembly into two and only two files — a fact of religious arithmetic worth pausing on. At the Day's sorting there is no third ammā, no miscellaneous drawer for the undecided, no provisional shelf. The Book's bifurcations are always total, and the particle here is their little gate: through it passes the whole human crowd, case by case, into complete classification. The *fa-* prefix stitches the sorting to what preceded, tying consequence-order to sight-order — the display stood revealed, *then* the sorting begins; first the common evidence, then the differentiated sentences. Procedure again: the Book's Day runs on sequence, not on explosion, and every particle of the sequence is deliberate.

**The Specification Chosen: One Preference Only**

When the charge is spelled, it is a single act of ranking: "and preferred the ˹fleeting˺ life of this world," (79:38). Not a tally of atrocities, not a curriculum of vices — one preference, named once, carries the file. The economy is stunning and needs to be received slowly: the whole difference between the two final homes is traced, in this sūrah's summation, to a choice of what to put first. A soul need not have built temples of cruelty; the preference alone, held and acted from, generates the file. This strips the deniers' favorite comfort — *we are no tyrants, no criminals* — of all function: the specification is set deliberately low and central, at the priority-level where every ordinary person lives.
verses.38:
> and preferred the ˹fleeting˺ life of this world

**Al-Ḥayāta d-Dunyā: The Name That Contains the Demotion**

What was preferred carries its own verdict inside its name: *ad-dunyā*, from a root of nearness and lowness — the *nearer, lower* life. Everything in the world's favor is packed into *near*: immediate, sensory, graspable, certain-in-hand. Everything against it sits in *lower*: a brief tenancy inside matāʿ, the provision-ware with the expiry built in. Even the translators' added gloss — *fleeting* — merely surfaces the Book's standing doctrine about this object: "These are the pleasures of this worldly life, but with Allah is the finest destination." (3:14).

**Wa-Ātharū: Preference as a Deed With Consequences**

The verb *āthara* means to prefer, to give precedence, to choose one thing over another — and its forensic power lies in treating preference as an *action*, something done, with the full moral weight of a deed. Men instinctively classify their cravings as weather: things that happen to them, conditions they live under. The verb re-files craving as conduct: at every fork of consequence, the self held two objects and *performed* a ranking, and rankings — repeated, embodied, funded — are choices as real as signatures. This transfers the locus of judgment inward, past behavior into ordering: the court does not merely ask what the file did; it asks what the file *put first*, reading conduct as the printout of priority. There is a precision here modern ears should catch: no one prefers in a void.

**The Arithmetic of the Broken Scale**

How does a rational creature mis-rank so catastrophically? And the Book marks where desire left as sole guide ends: "And who could be more astray than those who follow their desires with no guidance from Allah?" (28:50). *Misguidance*, in this analysis of the preference-pathology, is not chiefly an information failure — it is a weighting failure, guidance absent from the scale-pan.
verses.39:
> the Hellfire will certainly be ˹their˺ home

**Hiya: The Fire Itself — Nothing Standing Between**

Between the certainty and the home stands the pronoun *hiya* — *it, itself* — grammatically separable, semantically iron: the Hellfire, *it and no substitute*, is the shelter. The pronoun rules out every softening proxy: not a symbol of it, not a consequence merely *like* it, not a state of mind poetically its equal — *itself*. The Book's the teaching about the Last Day has always resisted being evaporated into metaphor by the squeamish of later ages, and this little pronoun does much of the resisting at the sentence-level: identity is asserted, not resemblance. A severe mercy hides inside the insistence: vagueness about *what exactly* the consequence is would be the final cruelty toward those still weighing the preference.

**The Mirrored Sentences of the Two Files**

The full architecture of the verdict now stands compare-able, since the second file receives, two verses later, a sentence built from the same materials: "Paradise will certainly be ˹their˺ home." (79:41). Same certainty, same *itself*, same *home* — the parallelism is the justice. No loaded grammar blesses one file and burdens the other; the sentence-form is scrupulously equal, and only the destination differs, because only the upstream lives differed.

**And the Counter-File Is Called**

The recitation does not leave the assembly standing at the first bench. Across the courtroom now comes the counter-construction, and with it the reversal of every term — the file "who were in awe of standing before their Lord" (79:40), the restraint laid upon the self, and the other *certainly*, the other home. The sūrah's bifurcation is about to double back over identical ground with opposite signs: where the first file leaned forward into the near-lower, the second stands back in awe of the Standing itself; where the first let the self run, the second forbids it. The two sentences are approaching that will measure every human record by the same pair of pivots — and the clause that opens the counter-file contains, in the phrase *standing before their Lord*, the whole secret the first file never kept in view.
verses.40:
> And as for those who were in awe of standing before their Lord and restrained themselves from ˹evil˺ desires

**Maqāma Rabbihi: Fear of the Standing-Place**

The awe's object is given with unusual concreteness: not God's wrath abstractly, not death generically, but *the standing before his Lord* — *maqām*, the stance-site, the place of being stood for review. To fear the Standing is to keep the specific event present: the summoned halt, the uncovered record, the master before whom posture is made perfect and nothing lean-on-able remains. Fear so specified is a remarkable psychological instrument — it is prospective, detailed, and personal (*his* Lord: the relationship named, not a terror of the void), and it re-values every present moment as pre-hearing material. Merchants fear audits only when audits are on the calendar; this awe pins the audit to every day, since the day's date is hidden — the concealment of the Hour, seen from this verse's side, is what makes the awe continuous rather than seasonal. The sūrah has been building this posture from its opening: "[The deniers'] hearts on that Day will be trembling ˹in horror˺," (79:8) — the trembling that arrives involuntarily at the event is, for the counter-file, voluntarily rehearsed before it: they trembled early, on purpose, in time.

**The Book's Own Double-Attestation of This Awe**

So load-bearing is this exact phrase — awe of the Standing — that the Book stakes a whole promise-scheme on it elsewhere in nearly the same words: "And whoever is in awe of standing before their Lord will have two Gardens." (55:46). Two attestation-points, one posture, paired reward-systems — and the doubling is itself a doctrine: the awe is not one sūrah's local theme but a fixed peg in the bargain-structure of salvation, repeated so that no attentive reader can misfile it as rhetoric.

**The Desire-God the Other File Serves**

What exactly is restrained, when desire is restrained, the Book diagnoses elsewhere at full depth, in its most psychiatric passage: "Have you seen ˹O Prophet˺ those who have taken their own desires as their god? ˹And so˺ Allah left them to stray knowingly, sealed their hearing and hearts, and placed a cover on their sight." (45:23). Desire enthroned is divinity misplaced — the analysis to end all analyses of the first file: their preference of the near-lower was, at bottom, worship; the hawā had the throne, the self had the liturgy, and the sealing of the organs was the enthronement's sacrament run to completion. Against that enthronement this verse's restraint is not prudery but counter-worship: each refusal of the desire is a dethronement-act, a daily denial of the rival god's claim, performed at the exact altar where the rival demands sacrifice.

**The Other Certainly, the Other Home**

The counter-file's suspension breaks with a verdict in parallel columns: "Paradise will certainly be ˹their˺ home." (79:41). Same grammar of certainty, same *itself*, same *home* — and at last the warm meaning of *maʾwā* returns to its native element: shelter after the road, refuge after the trial-ground, the Standing's exhaustion ended in residence.
verses.41:
> Paradise will certainly be ˹their˺ home

**Maʾwā Restored to Its Native Warmth**

When the first file received *home*, the word's ordinary warmth turned to frost: shelter with no release date, belonging as doom. Here the same noun returns home to itself. *Maʾwā* — refuge, the place sought through the whole journey, where the sought is finally housed — now carries its full native freight: the end of exposure, the road exhausted, the door that stays open to you forever. The re-warming of the identical noun across five verses is one of the sūrah's quietest feats: the audience has just heard *home* used as the horror-word and now watches the same letters glow again. In the watching learns the entire doctrine — the difference between the files was never in the *kind* of completeness each received, only in which completeness.

**But When? The Question Fired Back**

So the scene re-opens on the live audience, doing what warned audiences do when a warning lands too close: they ask for the date — "They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the Hour, 'When will it be?'" (79:42). The ask is the world's oldest deflection: convert the warning's *whether-you-are-ready* into the calendar's *when*, and argue with the calendar instead of with the soul. The recitation's final movement is heaven's management of exactly this maneuver: the knowledge redirected upward, the ministry redirected to awe, and the world's duration, at last sighting, deflated to an evening. The two homes have been named; it only remains for the Book, closing, to show what a whole lifespan spent disputing them looks like at the far end — brief as half a day.
verses.42:
> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ regarding the Hour, “When will it be?”

**Ayyāna Mursāhā: When Does the Ship Drop Anchor?**

The question's own wording is freighted with the answer it refuses to hear: *mursāhā* — its anchorage, its mooring, its settling-in — comes from a root used for ships coming to anchor, and *ayyāna* is simply *when*. The Hour is imagined, within the very vocabulary of the sneering question, as a vessel under sail toward a fixed berth: the askers themselves picture it as *arrival*, scheduled, inevitable, needing only the port-time. The image refutes the askers' motive by its logic. One does not ask a ship's mooring-time to dispute whether ships exist; the *when*-only posture is a concession that the arrival is certain — the whole controversy has silently shrunk to scheduling. Pagan cross-examination, at its cleverest stake-out, so already stands inside the preaching's frame: the Hour as an inbound vessel whose timetable is withheld.

**The Identical Question, Answered Elsewhere at Full Length**

The Book records the same interrogation — in one place, with its complete official answer appended, word-parallel from the outset: "They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the Hour, 'When will it be?' Say, 'That knowledge is only with my Lord. He alone will reveal it when the time comes. It is too tremendous for the heavens and the earth and will only take you by surprise.'" (7:187). The coordination between that answer and this sūrah's closing verses is exact to the point of manifest authorship: knowledge located with the Lord exclusively, disclosure timed by Him exclusively, arrival guaranteed as ambush. Yet another passage adds, in the same register: "People ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the Hour. Say, 'That knowledge is only with Allah. You never know, perhaps the Hour is near.'" (33:63) — and there the deflection is answered with urgency: the concealed date reframed as *perhaps near*, turning ignorance of the timetable from an excuse into the very engine of watchfulness.

**The Well-Worn Question-Habit of This Sūrah's Mockers**

Within this very chapter the asking-voice has been heard before, in the same deflecting key: "Will we really be restored to our former state," (79:10) — the mockery-question about bones and reassembly. Put the two questions side by side and their family resemblance is total: both aim interrogatives at the preaching's pressure-points, both substitute disputation for decision, both treat the unknowns of the afterlife as debating-matter to keep life's ledger unopened.

**The Prophet's Share of the Answer**

The first word of heaven's management of the question is a boundary, courteously but totally drawn around the Messenger himself: "But it is not for you to tell its time." (79:43). Before any speech to the askers, the Prophet's own relation to their demand is settled: the file's announcing is not in his brief.
verses.43:
> But it is not for you to tell its time

**The Jibrīl Precedent: The Ruling Demonstrated Live**

The Prophet enacted this verse's rule in the most famous examination-scene of the tradition. A man of striking appearance came to the sitting assembly, questioned the Prophet about Islam, faith, and excellence, and then asked about the Hour. The answer was the living form of this verse: *the one asked knows no more about it than the one asking* — and when the stranger departed, the Prophet identified him: that was Jibrīl, come to teach you your religion. The report stands in the most rigorously authenticated collections (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim). Its lesson-architecture is exact: the highest questioning-attendant heaven could send, dressed in human form, puts the schedule-question to the highest messenger earth had, and even in that summit-exchange the knowledge is declined — from both directions of the conversation at once. If angel-student and master-prophet share one ignorance on this item, the item's filing-location is established beyond appeal. The tradition leaves the community a permanent inoculation: its founding generation watched the limit honored at the very peak of revelatory access.

**The Mercy Built Into the Non-Disclosure**

The sealing of the date is not mere reserve; it is engineering for the soul's best functioning. A published deadline produces deadline-humans: long complacency, last-hour panic-repentance, devotion with the sincerity of tax-filing. A concealed appointment produces, in the serious, something far better than either: *standing* readiness, the life kept in order because the audit hovers over every day alike. The unknown date is so a distributional mercy — it spreads watchfulness evenly across a lifetime instead of concentrating it in a final weekend, and it keeps the market for religious theater small, since performance must be continuous to be timed right. The parallel-answer elsewhere in the Book turns the concealment into outright urgency: "You never know, perhaps the Hour is near." (33:63). Nearness-as-possibility replaces the calendar; the disciple is to live *as if* imminent what he cannot prove soon.

**Where the File Ends**

If neither asker nor asked holds the knowledge, one address remains at which the inquiry ends — and the recitation now names it, folding possession, custody, and final disclosure into a single phrase: "That knowledge rests with your Lord ˹alone˺." (79:44). The chain that began in the market's cross-examination ends in the divine cabinet, with the possessive *your Lord* holding the seal: the Messenger's own relationship is the letterhead on which the final classification of the Hour's file is stamped.
verses.44:
> That knowledge rests with your Lord ˹alone˺

**Ilā Rabbika Muntahāhā: The File's Final Page**

The noun *muntahā* is the terminating-point, the furthest reach of a thing — and here it marks where the Hour's knowledge-chain runs out: *unto your Lord is its end*. The image is administrative and total. Knowledge, in this depiction, is not a vapor available anywhere but a file with a chain-of-custody; trace the custody upward through every creaturely office and the chain hands you, at the summit, to a closed door whose keeper is named. The question so receives its most complete possible answer without receiving a date: not *nobody knows*, but *Somebody knows, and the knowledge stops there*. That distinction is the verse's center of gravity — agnosticism about the deity replaced by localization of the knowledge in Him.

**A Constitution for Creaturely Knowledge**

The verse legislates, beyond this case, a standing constitution: some files are creature-shareable and some are cabinet-only, and the Hour is the type-specimen of the second class. The parallel answer elsewhere in the Book states the constitution's disclosure-clause explicitly: He alone "will reveal it when the time comes." (7:187). Disclosure is itself scheduled — the appointment will be revealed *at* its appointment, so the teaching of the timing is timed together with the event, leaving no interval in which negotiations could run. Theology calls this the boundary of the unseen, and it functions as a permanent audit of religious claims: movements that traffic in the sealed class expose themselves by the very act of trafficking. Nor is the class arbitrary. The sealed files are consistently those whose disclosure would corrupt their function — the date that would manufacture insincerity, the timing that would abolish watchfulness.

So the commission comes down: "Your duty is only to warn whoever is in awe of it." (79:45). The exchange that opened as cross-examination closes as job-description.
verses.45:
> Your duty is only to warn whoever is in awe of it

**Innamā Anta Mundhir: The Ministry Compressed to One Office**

The particle *innamā* — *only, solely* — is the Book's celebrated instrument of relief, deployed at the Prophet's heaviest pressures: *your duty is only X*, where X is one clean deliverable instead of the unbounded obligations the opposition and the moment would pile on him. Here X is *mundhir*, warner: the office of issuing the alarm in advance of the danger. The compression cuts in several merciful directions at once. Against the askers: the warner-office explicitly excludes the timetable-desk they besieged, so their pressure-evidence is returned marked *not his department*. Against the sneerers' deeper demand — produce belief in us, manufacture our assent — it excludes that too: warning is deliverable; assent is the audience's own file. And against the Prophet's own burdened heart, the *only* is sheer relief: the commander of the message is not commanded the outcome. The same absoluteness that elsewhere makes the warning terrifying makes the office bearable: Day-outcomes are sealed matters in the cabinet of custody; the warner's shift ends each day with his warning delivered, his ledger closed.

**Warning as Discharged Duty, Not Failed Persuasion**

The relief-structure of the *only* deserves its full weight because the Prophet's context was attritional: years of warning delivered to a town where the respectable exacted mockery as their price of admission. Under siege like that, the natural metric of a ministry shifts from *warning delivered* to *converts produced* — and by the shifted metric, whole years looked like failure. The Book states the same consolation at its sternest in the patience-chapter: "So endure patiently, as did the Messengers of Firm Resolve. And do not ˹seek to˺ hasten ˹the torment˺ for the deniers." (46:35).

**And Then They See It**

One scene remains after the commission, and it belongs to the far side of the Hour's arrival: "On the Day they see it..." — where the calculation of a whole life's duration collapses to its retrospective measure, "no more than one evening or its morning" (79:46). The askers who demanded the schedule meet the schedule's arrival; and at the sight, every bargain about postponement closes out with the same figure on the ledger: the long delay they mocked in was, at audit, half a day.
verses.46:
> On the Day they see it, it will be as if they had stayed ˹in the world˺ no more than one evening or its morning

**Yawma Yarawnahā: The Sight That Ends Every Argument**

The verse's first move is optics: *the Day they see it*. The Hour, the disputed object of forty-five verses — mocked at the bones-question, besieged at the schedule-question, deflected through ritual cross-examination — here becomes simply *seen*, and seeing is the Book's terminal category. Every controversy of the chapter assumed the event's invisibility; the last verse removes the assumition that carried them all. Nothing more is litigated: the seeing-frame makes the whole preceding debate-readable in a single glance — the deniers' questions fossilize, in retrospect, into exhibits of the fog-era, when dispute was possible because sight was absent. And the pronoun *it* carries the authentic muffled quality of the inexplicable: the arrival needs no adjectives here, since vision itself is now transmitting. One verb of perception ends the longest argument of the chapter, which is also the longest argument in every skeptic's classroom: what was *whether* and *when* becomes *there* — and the whole scaffolding of postponement, built completely on un-seen-ness, comes down with the scaffolding's only pillar.

**The Book's Triple Attestation of the Collapsed Sum**

This estimation is repeated across the Book's separates scenes, in grades and witnesses. Emphatic elsewhere too: "˹as though˺ they had not stayed ˹in the world˺ except for an hour of a day" (10:45) — a hour, the shorter grade. And in the patience-chapter's parallel, the estimate stands at the same *hour of a day*, with the verdict attached: "Then, will anyone be destroyed except the rebellious people?" (46:35). The wicked, in the Byzantium-chapter's scene, go further — they *swear* to the figure: "the wicked will swear that they did not stay ˹in this world˺ more than a hour. In this way they were always deluded ˹in the world˺." (30:55). Three scenes, one figure-class — hour, evening, forenoon — and the oath in the third is the grimdest testimony of all: men will put it on oath, at the end, that the whole thing was that short. The Book reads back, over the oath, the diagnosis that they were *always* being eased onward — delusion-by-drift right up to its final day. Attestation so multiplied is doctrine: the compression is not one audience's impression but the species' shared audit-figure, sworn at last by those who fought it hardest.
